Keep investing from each paycheque during a crash, or pause until the market recovers? Following the units month by month

Follow a monthly contribution plan through a hypothetical market fall and recovery. Compare continuing with holding new money in cash until the old peak returns, see which months’ contributions did the most work, and find when the account is back above the money put in.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

A $20,000 balance is invested at a market peak and $500 is added at each month-end. The market falls 35% over 18 months, takes 42 more months to regain the old peak, and then grows 6% a year. The path is a hypothetical teaching shape, not the history of any index or fund, and no tax, fee or trading cost is modeled beyond the market path itself.

The central idea

Contributions made during a fall buy more units, so an account fed from pay can be back above its contributions well before the market regains its old peak. Pausing in cash avoids buying into further losses, but if a recovery comes, it waits for prices to return before buying. Neither choice makes a recovery happen, and money you may need soon should not be in the fund at all.

01

The month the statement turns red

Someone who invests a fixed amount from every paycheque into a balanced or equity fund will, sooner or later, open a statement showing that the account is worth less than the money put in. A common reaction is to stop the automatic contribution and keep the money in savings “until things settle down”. It feels like the cautious choice: why buy more of something that is falling?

This guide follows the arithmetic of that choice month by month. It is about new money arriving from earned pay, a stream of contributions that would not exist all at once. Deciding how to invest an existing lump sum, such as an inheritance or the proceeds of a sale, is a different question, compared in the lump-sum and phased-investing guide. Deciding whether to sell what is already invested is different again, and is tested in the exit-and-re-entry guide.

02

A hypothetical fall and recovery

The default scenario starts with CAD 20,000 already invested at a market peak and adds CAD 500 at each month-end. The market falls 35% over 18 months, so the price at the low is 65% of the old peak. It then takes 42 more months to climb back, regaining the old peak in month 60, and grows 6% a year afterwards. Each phase moves by the same percentage every month, a smooth shape chosen so that each effect can be seen; real markets move in jumps and false starts.

The comparison plan stops buying in month 1, holds every contribution in cash earning 2.5% a year, invests all of that cash in one purchase in month 60 when prices are back at the old peak, and then resumes the monthly contribution. Both plans put in exactly the same money: CAD 50,000 by month 60 and CAD 68,000 by month 96.

The recovery length is the decisive assumption, and it is the one nobody knows in advance. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site notes that markets have historically recovered from declines but that this can take months or several years. Change the inputs to try a faster bounce, a slower climb, or a recovery that does not arrive within the horizon.

03

What the two plans are worth along the way

The first chart plots both account values against the money put in. At the low in month 18, the continued plan is worth about CAD 20,400 against CAD 29,000 contributed; the paused plan is worth about CAD 22,159, because the CAD 9,000 held in cash did not fall. This is the stretch that makes pausing feel right.

The picture changes on the way back up. In month 60, when the market is exactly at its old peak, the continued plan is worth about CAD 57,500, while the paused plan is worth about CAD 51,898 after investing its cash at the peak price. By month 96 the values are about CAD 88,104 and CAD 81,432. The gap of roughly CAD 6,672 comes from the units that the monthly contributions bought below the old peak, less the interest the paused cash earned.

Set the cash rate to 0% and the paused plan ends at about CAD 79,172; the interest on the waiting cash is worth roughly CAD 2,260 here, not enough to close the gap. The result reverses if the market keeps falling or stays below the old peak for the whole horizon: then every unit bought during the fall is still at a loss, and holding cash would have been better. The model does not know which world you are in.

04

Back above your contributions before the market is back

The second chart compares two ratios: the market price as a share of the old peak, and the account value as a share of the money put in. With contributions continued, the account is back above its contributions in month 46, 14 months before the market regains its peak. At that point the market price is still about 13% below the peak. The paused plan crosses in month 53, helped by its cash interest and by the partial recovery of its starting balance.

The reason is the average price. The 60 contributions made until the peak returned bought their units at an average price of about 80% of the old peak. FINRA describes this as a benefit of regular investing in a decline: a fixed amount buys more units when prices are lower. The same page sets out the limits: holding cash and spreading purchases out often produces lower returns than investing at once, especially over longer periods, and per-transaction fees can erode returns.

The heatmap repeats the break-even month for different fall sizes and starting balances, keeping the 60-month round trip. Two patterns stand out. With no starting balance, the account is back above its contributions by month 32 or 33 whatever the depth of the fall, because a deeper fall also means cheaper units. With a starting balance of 240 monthly contributions, CAD 120,000 here, break-even moves out to month 55 or 56: a large existing balance follows the market, and new contributions are too small to pull the average down much. The earlier in a saving life a crash happens, the more the contributions dominate.

05

Which months’ contributions did the work

The third chart values each year’s block of purchases at the old peak price in month 60. Contributions made in months 13 to 24, around the low, show a paper gain of about 46.7%. Contributions in the first year of the fall show about 17.2%, and those made in the last year before the peak returned show only about 5.9%. The starting balance, bought at the peak, shows nothing.

These are the purchases that a pause skips. They also show why a pause is hard to undo in practice: the months that turned out best were the months when statements looked worst, and an investor waiting for “things to settle down” usually restarts after prices have risen. The waiting-for-a-dip guide tests the opposite habit, holding new money back until prices fall, and finds the same difficulty from the other side.

06

When pausing is the right decision

The case for continuing rests on contributions that can stay invested for many years. Pausing, or redirecting, can be the right call when the reason is your own cash flow rather than the market:

  • Your income is at risk. If a layoff or a cut in hours is plausible, building an emergency reserve comes first. The income-interruption guide sets a cash floor before contributions resume.
  • The money has a near deadline. Savings for a home deposit or tuition within a few years should not depend on a recovery date. The short-term goal guide shows how a loss close to a deadline cannot be waited out.
  • High-interest debt is growing. Paying down a credit card charging 20% or more is a known return; a fund’s return is not.
  • The fund was the wrong choice to begin with. If the fall revealed a risk level you cannot live with, change the mix deliberately, for future contributions, rather than stopping and starting with the headlines. The balanced-fund crash guide compares mixes.

Costs matter too. Check whether your plan charges a commission or fee on each purchase; if it does, many small purchases can cost more than a few larger ones. The fund’s own ongoing fees apply to every dollar invested either way, and are already inside the market path in this model.

07

The account and the fund are separate decisions

Contributions into a TFSA or RRSP use room that is not otherwise used, and growth inside those accounts is not taxed while it stays there; pausing does not normally lose the room, which carries forward, but cash parked outside the account earns taxable interest. In a non-registered account, every month’s purchase adds to the adjusted cost base, and units bought near the low carry larger future gains, which are taxed only when units are sold. The fund itself does not change its tax treatment; the account’s rules decide it.

None of this predicts the next crash or its recovery. The OSC cautions that diversification provides reasonable protection in normal markets but can be less effective in extreme conditions, when most investments fall together, and warns against selling in a downturn. The decision that holds up in most scenarios is less about timing the market and more about making sure each contribution is money you will not need before a recovery could plausibly arrive.
